https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Killing of Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil was a war crime, say rights groups. Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/AP View image in fullscreen Killing of Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil was a war crime, say rights groups. Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Rights and freedom Israel Israeli strike that killed journalist in Lebanon was war crime, say rights groups Investigation by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and Legal Agenda shows Israel deliberately attacked Amal Khalil and colleague Zeinab Faraj knowing they were civilians Supported by About this content William Christou Thu 6 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 02.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Israeli strike that killed Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil and injured her colleague Zeinab Faraj in April was a war crime, three rights organisations said on Thursday. Investigations from Human Rights Watch (HRW), Amnesty International and Legal Agenda showed that Israel deliberately and directly attacked Khalil and Faraj, with apparent knowledge that they were civilians. The organisations called for the attacks to be investigated as war crimes, while HRW called for states to halt arm sales to Israel and put targeted sanctions on Israeli officials responsible for ongoing crimes. Deliberate attacks on civilians, which both journalists were, is a war crime. Israel has killed at least 15 journalists in Lebanon and 210 in Gaza since 2023, according to the UN human rights office . The reports also indicated that Israel delayed Lebanese ambulances from reaching Khalil and Faraj for hours – at one pointing dropping stun grenades on Lebanese Red Cross workers and firing on their ambulances. The delay in rescue might have led to Khalil’s death, as hospital reports indicate that she might have still been alive hours after an Israeli strike toppled a building on top of her and Faraj. “The evidence is clear that the Israeli military knew, or should have, that Faraj and Khalil were civilians, but attacked them anyway, and then prevented paramedics from rescuing them for hours,” said Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon researcher at Human Rights Watch. Israel said it “regrets any harm caused to journalists,” and that the journalists were killed “as part of a series of events” during which two Hezbollah military operatives were killed. There was about two hours between the initial strike that killed the two men Israel said were in Hezbollah, and a second strike that targeted a building the journalists were sheltering in. Amal Khalil was a 42-year-old journalist working for al-Akhbar, a Lebanese newspaper, while Zeinab Faraj was a 21-year-old freelance camerawoman and photojournalist. Both had been active in covering the war in Lebanon over the last three years. View image in fullscreen Zainab, the sister of Amal Khalil, mourns over her coffin in Baysariyeh, southern Lebanon. Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/AP On 22 April 2026, the pair drove to the village of al-Tiri, south Lebanon, to verify reports that Israeli troops had left the area. They drove behind a car carrying Ali Nabil Bazzi, a municipal official of the city of Bint Jbeil, as well as Mohammed Hourani, a friend of the mayor. Al-Tiri was in what Israel calls its “security zone” in southern Lebanon, which its troops occupy. Amnesty said that despite the Israeli military calling it a military zone and barring people from going there, it is still required to distinguish between civilians and combatants. At 2.25pm, after entering al-Tiri, the car carrying Bazzi and Hournai was struck, killing the men. Khalil called the Lebanese civil defence and requested assistance. The civil defence drove to the entry of the village, where they were told to stop at a military checkpoint while they waited for authorisation from the Israeli military to enter the village safely. Rescue crews operating in areas of south Lebanon where fighting is taking place or which the Israeli military occupies must coordinate with the “mechanism”, a deconfliction channel, to get safe passage. Among others, the Israeli military must give approval for requests for civil defence to get safe passage. By 5pm, the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon had given a safe route for civil defence to follow to enter the town, but Israel had not yet given its approval. While waiting for the civil defence to arrive, Faraj and Khalil left their car and sought shelter elsewhere. Israeli quadcopters circled low overhead while the two journalists waited, Faraj said. “The drones came extremely close through the roof, less than a metre from my face and Amal’s,” she said. At 3.31pm, a member of the Lebanese civil defence called Khalil and urged her to get into her car and drive out of the village, as he had not yet received permission from the mechanism to enter the village. Around nine minutes later, Israel struck the journalists’ car, injuring both women. “Glass and debris flew towards us. My ear felt like it burst. She [Amal Khalil] was bleeding heavily from the nose and head and had shrapnel wounds in her arm and thigh; she couldn’t move her leg,” Farj said. The two women crawled into a nearby building for shelter. They both continued calling people, asking for assistance, but were told they could not be rescued until authorisation was given from the mechanism. At 4.25pm, Israel conducted a third strike, bombing the building where they were sheltering, collapsing it and burying both women under the rubble. At 5pm, permission was given to the Lebanese Red Cross to enter the village. They were able to evacuate Faraj, who had a fractured skull, severe injuries to her right leg and eye, and a crushed hand. Rescuers could not rescue Khalil, who was trapped under rubble. The rescuers came under attack by an Israeli quadcopter, which dropped a stun grenade near them. Witnesses also said they heard bursts of gunfire during the evacuations, and HRW reviewed photographs of bulletholes in the ambulances consistent with small arms fire. The rescuers were forced to withdraw with only Faraj. The Israeli military finally granted the request for rescue crews to re-enter the town at 8.15pm. Khalil’s body was recovered at 11pm. An examination of her body at the nearby Tebnine hospital showed that she probably died at 7pm – two-and-a-half hours after she was struck for the last time. She was trapped under the rubble during that time, waiting to be rescued, while the Israeli military prevented rescue crews from saving her life. All three organisations have demanded accountability for Khalil’s killing, and described it as part of a larger pattern of impunity by the Israeli military towards civilians. “The impunity enjoyed by Israeli forces for the killing of journalists and other civilians in Lebanon over the past three years has enabled the Israeli military to continue with its unlawful airstrikes, including direct attacks on civilians,” said Heba Morayef, director for the Middle East and north Africa at Amnesty International. “It is well past time that the international community impose a comprehensive arms embargo on Israel,” Morayef added. Why it matters: The plan, which Bessent dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast,” is aimed at ratcheting up pressure on the Iranian regime amid the current “no war, no deal” limbo. U.S. officials say the expanded “secondary” sanctions are expected to be the main course of action against Iran until at least after the midterm elections, when a new military campaign could again be on the table. What he said: “ Let there be no ambiguity as to the position of the United States,” Bessent said at a news conference. “An economic engagement of any kind with this murderous regime will expose those responsible to the full reach of American power.” Bessent did not give a deadline for compliance, but said, “I’m not going to set a timeline, but we do not have infinite patience here.” “No one is above this,” Bessent said in response to a question about whether the initiative would encompass China. “This is economic asphyxiation of this regime … and no one should test our resolve.” Zoom in: Bessent said the U.S. is expanding the categories of secondary sanctions to the fields of digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. The exact location has not been revealed, due to security concerns, but sources have told the Telegraph that the facility was disabled “while staff fought to bring it back online” after the attack. Read more “The Key to Lasting Peace in the Region Is in Iran” Franck Radjai, a research director at the CNRS at the University of Montpellier and president of the Association of Academics for Freedom in Iran, fled Iran in 1983 after personally experiencing the repression of the mullahs’ regime; his sister had been executed two years earlier. For more than 40 years, he has followed developments in his country. He hopes that the Iranian people can bring about regime change themselves. Amid geopolitical challenges, the economic consequences of the Strait of Hormuz crisis, negotiations between the United States and Iran, and the human rights situation, Franck Radjai discusses the Iranian people’s resistance and their hopes, seeking to shed light on the reality of Iran. Negotiations between Iran and the United States are underway. How should the escalation of demands between the two sides be interpreted? Since the beginning of the war, the reasons officially given by Donald Trump, who said it was to help the Iranians, are obviously not really the main reasons. This is a geopolitically important region. And that is perhaps clearer to everyone now. Whatever the reasons for its outbreak, this is another war. It is worth remembering that shortly beforehand there was the 12-day war (editor’s note: June 13–24, 2025), followed by attacks on Western interests through proxies across the region, not to mention hostage-taking. This is the regime’s usual chaotic behavior as it seeks to subjugate others and create a form of deterrence extending far beyond its borders. Read more UPDATE: 7:00 AM CEST Over 600 Political Prisoners in Ahvaz’s Sheiban Prison Amid Overcrowding, Summary Trials, And Death Sentences A comprehensive report released by the Iran Human Rights Society on August 22, 2026, reveals that more than 600 political and ideological prisoners are currently detained under dire conditions in Sheiban Central Prison in Ahvaz. Following extensive waves of arrests by regime security and intelligence forces across Khuzestan Province, the facility’s total inmate population has surged to over 4,000—more than double its official 2,000-person capacity. The vast majority of those recently detained are young men aged 18 to 25, who are being subjected to summary, video-conferenced mass trials inside the prison, denied independent legal counsel, and handed sentences ranging from lengthy prison terms to capital punishment. Intelligence units of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and state security apparatuses have carried out extensive nighttime raids targeting residential neighborhoods across Khuzestan Province, particularly in Ahvaz, Shadegan, Izeh, Behbahan, and Masjed Soleyman. Hundreds of young citizens have been arbitrarily detained without judicial warrants and initially held in undisclosed interrogation centers before being transferred to Sheiban Prison. Families have systematically been denied information regarding the official charges, detainee whereabouts, or legal status. The report documents that judicial proceedings are being conducted inside the prison via video conference in group formats, severely undermining the right to a fair defense. Detainees are barred from reviewing their case files or consulting with independent defense attorneys. Read more Iran: Female Prisoner, 35, Executed in the Central Prison of Karaj In the early hours of Sunday, August 23, 2026, the Iranian regime executed a female prisoner, identified as “Maryam” in the Central Prison of Karaj . Maryam, 35 and a native of Karaj, had previously been arrested on charges of murder and sentenced to death by the clerical regime’s judiciary. Over the past week, she was subjected to severe psychological torment. She was initially transferred to solitary confinement to face execution, but after a temporary stay, she was returned to the general ward. However, prison authorities transferred her back to solitary confinement on Saturday, August 22, and carried out her death sentence early Sunday morning. Maryam’s execution in the Central Prison of Karaj brings the total number of women executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026 to at least 22. Read more Iran’s Regime Infighting: A Sign of a Deepening Crisis of Survival The intensifying disputes within Iran’s ruling establishment raise a fundamental question: Are these merely factional disagreements, or do they point to something far more consequential? The answer lies beyond the immediate quarrels between competing power centers. In political systems, the escalation of internal conflicts is often a reflection of deeper structural crises. When a government faces widespread public discontent, economic hardship, social unrest, political instability, and the erosion of its social base, disagreements within the ruling elite inevitably become sharper. This is precisely what is increasingly visible in Iran. The regime’s internal confrontations are not simply disputes over policy or administrative methods. They increasingly resemble a struggle over responsibility, power, and ultimately political survival. A government with broad social support can generally absorb internal disagreements. Competing factions can negotiate, compromise, and resolve disputes through established political mechanisms. Read more Iran Links Strait of Hormuz Shipping to Sanctions Relief as Regional Bypass Routes Expand TEHRAN — The Strait of Hormuz is no longer merely a site of naval confrontation or a threat to halt tanker traffic after the Iran-U.S. war. Tehran is now linking the normalization of shipping through the waterway to a broader set of demands, ranging from lifting the blockade and easing sanctions to the implementation of previous U.S. commitments, effectively seeking to turn its geographic power in Hormuz into bargaining leverage . Donya-e Eqtesad , in interviews with four international affairs experts, described Tehran’s current policy as resting on three tools: negotiations, military deterrence and economic resistance . Hormuz is the point where all three converge; Iran can place the normalization of traffic on the negotiating table, retain the threat of disruption as backing for diplomacy, and buy time for bargaining by enduring economic pressure. Rahman Ghahremanpour, an international affairs analyst, said of the choice facing Tehran : “There are currently two views regarding Iran’s approach to U.S. economic pressure and blockade against our country: the first is escalation, and the second is a return to the agreement, with the consensus within the ruling establishment leaning more toward a return to the agreement.” The issue, therefore, is no longer simply whether Iran can close Hormuz; the question is what it will receive in return for normalizing it again. https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg delivers a speech, as a giant image of Ray-Ban smart glasses appears on screen, in Menlo Park, California, on 27 September 2023. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters View image in fullscreen Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg delivers a speech, as a giant image of Ray-Ban smart glasses appears on screen, in Menlo Park, California, on 27 September 2023. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters Technology US police fear Meta smart glasses could be used to secretly record them Exclusive: Documents show officers from Maine to California worry Meta’s camera-equipped glasses will be used either to secretly record them or aid acts of terrorism Johana Bhuiyan Tue 8 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 06.04 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In January, the New York Police Department’s counterterrorism unit sent out a memo warning police officers about a new potential “security and counterintelligence” threat: Ray-Ban Meta glasses. The memo directed officers to “conduct thorough inspections of all eyewear permitted within inmate cells” and cautioned that people who have been arrested could use these glasses, equipped with small cameras and microphones, to record inside police facilities. The memo cited two examples of such videos posted on social media. “The ability to covertly record inside a law enforcement or detention facility, could result in a security risk if proprietary information about cell layouts, camera placements, or officer patrol/site protection routines are released,” the memo read. The NYPD memo is one of a dozen, previously unreported and reviewed by the Guardian, that showed law enforcement agencies across the US are increasingly concerned about the potential for smart glasses to be used against them. Officers from Maine to California worry the technology will be used either to secretly record officers and facilities or to aid in the execution of crimes and acts of terrorism. One of the videos, taken with smart glasses and posted to TikTok in July 2025, offered a rare peek into a South Carolina detention center that had been the subject of a federal investigation over unsafe conditions. “Everyone here is trying to figure out what’s going on with my glasses, why my light is blinking,” the user said about other detainees in the video. “People don’t know about Meta glasses.” He filmed a dingy shower, the inside of holding cells, an overcrowded cafeteria, and several other detainees as they slept, ate, or walked, all seemingly unaware of being recorded. Detention facilities in the US typically confiscate any and all devices that would be capable of recording video footage. Some Meta smart glasses have gone unnoticed, though. The glasses are discreet and can pass as a regular pair of Ray-Bans or Oakleys. Their main differentiator is a small blinking light in the corner of the frame that is activated when the glasses are recording. The covertly recorded videos prompted the NYPD’s intelligence and counterterrorism bureau, a specialized unit that works with the FBI to monitor and prevent terrorist threats, to send out the January memo to other police departments. The glasses “may appear as ordinary prescription eyewear”, the memo read. US police and federal agents are not alone in their fear. Concern among the public and privacy experts over Meta’s smart glasses, widely dubbed “ pervert glasses ”, is growing. The technology enables its wearers to record people without their consent and has already been used to harass people . Documents obtained by Property of the People, a non-profit that works to increase government transparency, show law enforcement have grown as equally worried as everyday people about being filmed without their knowledge. Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of Property of the People, said the documents show that law enforcement wants the exclusive right to use surveillance technology and cameras to monitor the public without those cameras being turned back on them. “These agencies surveil the public incessantly, but the moment we can watch them back, it’s deemed a security threat,” Shapiro said. “When only the government is allowed to hold the camera, that’s not security. It’s impunity.” “The potential for smart glasses to be used by residents and the general public to conduct surveillance and other nefarious activities has introduced additional risks and concerns in Department of Corrections and law enforcement facilities,” read a memo distributed in June 2026 by Maine’s fusion center. Fusion centers are Department of Homeland Security facilities spread across the country as surveillance hubs that collect and analyze what the DHS describes as “threat-related” information from local law enforcement, private companies and other state and federal agencies. “Some smart glasses can leverage AI software including facial recognition, which could lead to doxing of publicly available information or connections to law enforcement officers,” the Maine document continued. Other memos expressing concerns about Meta smart glasses originated from the DHS’s joint counterterrorism assessment team and fusion centers nationwide, including in San Diego, California, Tennessee, Virginia, Maine and New York. Those fears have been enough to prompt federal agencies to bar their own employees from using the smart glasses in the workplace. In August, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency said that smart glasses qualify as body-worn cameras, which means they can’t be worn in the “federal workspace”, according to a memo the New York Times obtained . The “use of Meta Glasses or similar devices could unintentionally capture, record or transmit sensitive information”, the memo, written by ICE’s acting director David Venturella, read. Meta says its glasses “are designed to be noticed”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives after newsletter promotion “Every pair has a bright white LED that blinks when a photo or video is taken for your gallery, it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or tampers with the LED, the camera is disabled,” said Meta spokesperson Dina El-Kassaby. Beyond being filmed without their consent, law enforcement agencies are also cautioning that these glasses may be used to aid in planning or “reconnaissance” for violent acts of terrorism or “hostile pre-operational surveillance”. A January 2025 NYPD memo cited the New Year’s Day terror attack in New Orleans, when a man rammed his truck into a crowd on Bourbon Street, killing 14 and wounding 35 people. The FBI had alerted local agencies like the NYPD that the perpetrator of the attack biked around Bourbon street twice at the end of 2024 wearing smart glasses. The FBI alleges the perpetrator conducted “pre-attack target reconnaissance”. Officers should be aware of and report individuals “acting in a suspicious manner observed wearing what may be smart glasses”, the memo states. Evan Greer, the executive director of digital advocacy non-profit Fight for the Future, said they’re not surprised police are concerned about the technology being used against them or to cause harm. “Surveillance makes all of us less safe,” Greer said. “There’s no such thing as Meta glasses that are only for the good guys. ” The French quarter is a highly trafficked tourist area, Meta spokesperson El-Kassaby said, arguing that the perpetrator could have filmed the French Quarter with any other recording device including a phone. The concern over Meta’s smart glasses are part of a broader concern expressed by law enforcement over the ways the proliferation of artificial intelligence-backed technology may impinge on police activity, the documents show. Law enforcement are at once looking for ways to use AI for investigative purposes and warning against public opposition to its use. In an August 2025 document, the NYPD wrote that while new AI technology could “significantly transform day-to-day police operations” that police would also need to address public fears about the use of advanced tech in policing. The memo was a response to “ AI 2027 ”, a paper written by a former OpenAI researcher and other industry experts proffering what the future of AI development could look like and the effect it will have on society. It warns that AI opposition could result in “anti-tech violent extremist activity” and civil unrest over job losses, the widespread use of deepfake technology, and loss of trust in government and tech. Anti-tech violent extremist activity isn’t a formal DHS designation for categories of terrorism but has recently cropped up in law enforcement messaging about a broad spectrum of extremist opposition to AI. Experts worry it could serve to criminalize all anti-tech opposition and the constitutionally protected right to protest. Photograph: Family Handout/PA View image in fullscreen The inquest into the death of Noah Woods was opened and adjourned on Friday. Photograph: Family Handout/PA Suffolk Noah Woods, three, died after leaving playground through gap in fence, inquest told Boy became separated from a relative in Suffolk and went in the direction of a pond where he was later found dead Emine Sinmaz and PA Media Fri 25 Sep 2026 06.49 EDT Last modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 06.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A three-year-old boy who was found dead in a pond after going missing from a playground had left the play area “through a gap in the fence”, an inquest heard. Noah Woods became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close, Brantham, on the afternoon of 15 September, Suffolk police said. About 1,300 members of the public joined a search to find Noah, who police said was non-verbal, partially deaf and had been undergoing an assessment for autism. Met police divers recovered his body from what is known locally as Decoy Pond on the afternoon of 16 September. Suffolk police said his death was not being treated as suspicious. An inquest into Noah’s death was opened and adjourned in Ipswich on Friday. DCI Matthew Connick told the hearing that on 15 September, Noah, of East Bergholt, Suffolk, was being “looked after by relatives and this was part of a normal routine for Noah”. He said they walked to an under-fives play area and CCTV footage in the park “showed Noah playing with his relative”. The first CCTV footage was timed at 2.13pm and he was last seen playing at 2.37pm, said Connick, who added the CCTV “is motion-activated so doesn’t provide continuous footage”. He said the relative, who was not named at the hearing, had provided a statement to police. The officer said Noah “left through a gap in the fence leading to the memorial garden where he left through an open gate”. He said Noah went in the direction of Decoy Pond and he was “being closely followed by his relative who was trying to keep up with him”. He said the relative “shouted after him” but after 200 metres Noah could not be seen. “Police were called and a large-scale search operation began,” Connick said. He said Noah was found by a Met police diver “approximately 5 metres from the bank and within submerged tree roots”. The depth was estimated at 1.8 metres at that point, he added. A postmortem at Addenbrooke’s hospital mortuary in Cambridge recorded his medical cause of death as pending further investigation, Connick said. Noah’s death was confirmed at 4.31pm by paramedics and his identity was formally confirmed by his mother, Charlie Peck, at Ipswich hospital that evening. An assistant coroner for Suffolk, Jyoti Gill, said at the outset of the hearing, which was not attended by the boy’s family: “I would like to express my deepest condolences to Noah’s family and friends and all those affected by Noah’s death.” She said at the end of the six-minute hearing: “The inquest is adjourned to a date to be fixed in due course. Once again, my deepest condolences.” Noah’s father, Rhys Woods , paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group last week. He described Noah as the “sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give”, and added: “We are going to miss him so very much.” Football players also paid tribute to Noah during Everton’s home match against Ipswich Town on Saturday by wearing black armbands.
